Chapter 8. The First Weeks: Hopes, Illusions, and the Reality of War.
When the war finally broke out, hardly anyone really knew what was coming. In those first few weeks, it almost felt surreal—like everything was happening in a dream. People clung to the idea that this conflict would be short, maybe even glorious. Newspapers were filled with stirring stories of heroism, and politicians promised everyone they'd be celebrating victory by Christmas.
Overnight, the world that everyone thought they knew—the routines, the certainties—just seemed to disappear.
Out in the countryside, you could see farmers pausing their work, watching long columns of soldiers marching by. Their uniforms were spotless, their spirits high. And in the cities, families gathered at train stations, saying goodbyes that were wrapped in brave smiles, even while worry flickered behind their eyes. For so many, the war still felt like an adventure—a chance to prove courage and loyalty.
But the truth quickly turned out to be very different. The German army, sticking to its carefully laid plans, swept through Belgium and pushed into France. The fighting was fierce—and the cost, devastating. Civilians ran from their homes, caught in the middle of advancing armies. In Belgium, stories of terrible atrocities spread like wildfire, fueling both anger and fear.
Over on the Eastern Front, Russian and German soldiers clashed in battles that were chaotic and brutally intense. The sheer scale of the conflict was unlike anything anyone had ever seen before. Suddenly, everything people thought they could count on was crumbling. Commanders found themselves struggling to keep up with new technology—machine guns, heavy artillery, barbed wire—making the battlefield far deadlier than anyone could have imagined.
Down in the trenches, life was harsh beyond words. Mud, hunger, and the constant threat of danger became the new normal. The hope of a quick victory faded fast. Letters sent home were filled with stories of exhaustion and loss. The war stopped being just a test for armies—it became a test for entire societies. Governments started rationing food, imposing new rules, and calling up more and more men. Suddenly, what happened at home mattered just as much as what happened on the front lines.
For so many people, those first weeks of war shattered everything they thought they knew. The dream of a quick, glorious fight was gone—replaced by a grim determination just to hold on. The world had changed, and there was no turning back.
